about.text: I'm {given}. I don't have a trade yet. Mum says I will when I'm bigger.
{name}. I've been in {settlement} longer than the well.
{given}'s the name. I keep the {job}'s hours and the {job}'s worries.
I'm {given}! I'm the {job}, and I love it.
I'm {given}. We've not much, but we get by.
{name}. Don't look at the patches; look at the work.
{name}. My family has held land about {settlement} for generations.
I am {name}, and {settlement} is under my protection.
{name}. I keep the watch here, and the watchmen.

about.job.text: I build. Houses, walls, the odd bridge. Every block goes where the plan says.
The fields keep this town fed. I keep the fields.
I walk the woods and bring back timber. Plant two for every one I fell.
Stone's in my bones. I cut it from the hill.
Up before the gulls, out on the water.
Sheep, goats, the odd stubborn cow. They're good company.
I track game in the hills. Quiet work.
Tables, doors, carts, cradles. If it's wood, I make it.
Bricks, dressed stone, glass. The town's bones and skin.
Tools, nails, hinges, and the dies the mint strikes coin with.
Bread at dawn, pies by noon. I'm the reason this town smells so good.
Ale, cider, a little something stronger for winter.
I keep the inn. Beds for travellers and the best stories in town.
I keep the stall. Buy low, sell fair, that's my motto.
I strike the coin and keep the treasury. Every bit is accounted for.
I keep the watch. Nothing comes through that gate without me knowing.
I tend the altar and the people who come to it.
I read, I write, I remember. Somebody has to.
Letters, parcels, gossip. I carry them all between the towns.
Wool to thread, thread to cloth, cloth to coats.
No trade, these days. I keep the house and mind everyone's business.
I work the mine. Down the adit before sunrise, up after dark, and the hill a little emptier each day.
Every gallery we cut, we prop and light behind us. The dark doesn't forgive a lazy miner.
I carry. Stone to the mason, logs to the mill, grain to the granary. My back is this town's road.
Somebody has to move it all from where it's dug to where it's wanted. That's me.
I burn wood slow under turf till it's charcoal. Smells like smoke for days, but the smith can't work without me.
A good clamp burns three days and you don't sleep for any of them.
Clay in, bricks out. The kiln never quite cools.
Every roof tile in {settlement} came through my kiln.
Sand and fire and breath, and out comes a window. I never tire of it.
Glass is patient work. Hurry it and it cracks, and so does your temper.
Ore and charcoal go in, iron comes out. Hot, hard work, but the whole town stands on it.
I keep the furnace fed. Let it go cold and the smiths have nothing to hammer.
Hides to leather. It stinks, I know. Everyone tells me. Everyone wears my boots, too.
The vats need a month. Leather can't be rushed.
I'm the butcher. Clean cuts, fair weight, no questions about the sausages.
Meat for the inn, meat for the market, and the hides go to the tanner. Nothing wasted.
Candles. Every window lit in {settlement} after dark, that's my wax.
Dip, cool, dip again. Forty times for a good church candle.
I keep the bees. They know me, mostly. The honey's worth the stings.
Smoke them gentle, take only what they can spare. That's the whole secret.
Rags and reeds become paper here. The scholars can't write a word without me.
A sheet a minute when the press is running well.
Woad blue, madder red, weld yellow. My hands are every colour but my own.
A good dye takes; a bad one runs in the first rain. Mine take.
I work the salt pans. Sun and wind do most of it; I rake and carry the rest.
Salt keeps the fish and the meat through winter. Worth its weight, they say. Nearly.
I dig clay from the bank. Mud to the knees, but the kiln wants it.
Good clay's grey and sticky and smells of the river. You learn to know it.
Boats. Keel first, ribs after, then the planking. A good one outlives its builder.
Every boat on the water here, I built or mended.
I trade between the towns. Buy where it's plenty, sell where it's dear.
The roads are my shop. Timber one way, salt the other.
I'm the healer. Herbs, splints, a kind word. Mostly the kind word.
Come see me if you're hurt. Don't wait till it festers like the last fool did.
I play, I sing, I tell stories. Somebody has to keep this town from dying of boredom.
Come to the inn tonight. I've a new song about a dragon and a very foolish knight.
I keep the bathhouse. Hot water, clean towels, and the best gossip in town.
You'd be surprised how much nicer folk are to a stranger who's had a bath.
I keep the stables. Horses to hire, horses to buy, horses to mind.
A horse knows a liar. I trust them more than most men.
I'm the reeve. Rolls, rents, roads and quarrels. If it's the town's business, it's mine.
I keep the rolls of {settlement}. Every house, every field, every debt.
I sit in judgement. The law is the law, whoever you are.
Fines for the small things, the pillory for the shameful, the rope for the worst. I take no pleasure in the last.
I keep the keys to the cells. Nobody leaves before their time.
Quiet in the cells today. I like it quiet.
I buy and sell odds and ends. Don't ask where things come from and I won't ask where they're going.
A little of this, a little of that. Honest prices for... honest goods.
I keep the lord's household: the stores, the accounts, the servants. Everything that isn't the sword.
The treasury balances. It always balances. I see to it.
These lands and the people on them are in my keeping. I hold court in the hall each morning.
A lord who doesn't know his people's names doesn't deserve their rents.

about.spouse: My {spouse} and I have been together for years.

about.spouse.text: {spouse}? Oh, we argue like cats, but I'd be lost without them.
Have you met my {spouse}? The finest person in {settlement}.

about.children: Our little ones keep us busy: {children}.

about.children.text: {children}. Mine, all of them, and every one a handful.
